query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A small addition of Sn to single‐phase fcc FeCoNi will induce the nucleation of a secondary, harder BCC phase (or nano‐precipitates) within the fcc matrix, and these features will act as domain wall pinning centers to increase the coercive field beyond 100 Oe.
generation.material_initial_state: Single‐phase fcc FeCoNi (or a closely matched high‐entropy alloy derivative) that exhibits high saturation magnetization but low coercivity (≲100 Oe).
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor amount of Sn (e.g., up to ~10 atomic percent relative to a base alloy such as FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8) during alloy synthesis by arc-melting followed by an appropriate heat treatment to promote phase separation.
generation.conditions: The alloy should be processed under conditions comparable to those used for high-entropy alloys – ensuring minimal changes to the overall composition except for the Sn addition, with subsequent annealing to facilitate the formation of a dual-phase microstructure. Measurements should be carried out at room temperature under standard magnetic characterization conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale or microscale BCC phase precipitates (or a partial transformation of the matrix) embedded within the fcc host.
generation.mechanism: The Sn addition promotes a metastable phase transformation that results in a dual-phase microstructure. The emerging BCC phase has a higher magnetocrystalline anisotropy and provides effective pinning sites for domain walls, thereby increasing the coercive field without significantly compromising the high saturation magnetization characteristic of the fcc phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will show an increased coercive field—well above the typical <100 Oe—while maintaining a high saturation magnetization compared to the single-phase fcc FeCoNi baseline.
generation.baseline: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi with high saturation magnetization and coercive field near or below 100 Oe.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to work as long as the Sn addition is kept small enough not to overly dilute the magnetic moment or induce unwanted phases. It applies to alloys processed by arc melting and conventional annealing, where controlled phase separation into fcc and BCC (or comparable hard magnetic precipitates) can occur.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Sn content required and the detailed kinetics of the phase transformation are not fully established; furthermore, the balance between maintaining high saturation magnetization and raising coercivity may require optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of alloys: one set of single-phase fcc FeCoNi (or its well-matched derivative) and another with a minor Sn addition under identical synthesis and annealing conditions. Characterize the microstructure via XRD and electron microscopy to check for BCC (or nano‐precipitate) phase formation. Perform magnetic hysteresis measurements to determine coercivity and saturation magnetization.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to detect the presence of a secondary BCC phase or precipitates
Transmission or scanning electron microscopy (TEM/SEM) for microstructural analysis
Magnetic hysteresis loops to measure coercivity (Hc) and saturation magnetization (Ms)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with Sn addition does not show a statistically significant increase in coercivity (i.e., remains below or around 100 Oe) or if no evidence of a secondary BCC phase or nano-precipitates is observed compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work exhibits the effects of Sn addition on the magnetic properties and microstructure of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The results show all the samples consist of a mixed structure of face-centered-cubic (FCC) phase and body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nano-precipitates in BCC matrix. It also shows that the Curie temperatures (Tc) of the FCC phase and the saturation magnetization (Ms) of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs increase greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases after the addition of Sn into FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA. The thermomagnetic curves indicate that the phases of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs will transform from FCC with low Tc to BCC phase with high Tc at temperature of 600–700 K. This work provides a new idea for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs for their potential application as soft magnets to be used at high temperatures.

In this work, the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs were prepared by vacuum arc-melt casting. Effects of Sn content on the phase constitution and magnetic properties were studied. All the samples are composed of FCC and BCC phases, whereas some unknown phases appear with the addition of Sn. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nanoprecipitates in the BCC matrix. Moreover, the Ms increases greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases with the increasing of x for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs. The addition of Sn can obviously increase the Curie temperature of the FCC phase. The phase of alloys with a mixture of FCC and BCC will transform from FCC to BCC phase at high temperature, leading to an increase of magnetization. They can be used as new soft magnetic materials at high temperatures.
